title: Boundary-Guided Mammographic Radiomics for Molecular Subtype Risk Stratification in Breast Cancer
abstract: This work proposes a multi-stage interpretable framework for mammography-based molecular subtype-oriented risk stratification in breast cancer, focusing on visible mass lesions with segmentable tumor boundaries. The framework integrates a Boundary-Enhanced module within an attention-based U-Net architecture to improve tumor boundary delineation. Morphological and radiomics descriptors capturing shape, margin-related geometry, intensity, and texture heterogeneity are then extracted from the segmented tumor region and used for machine-learning-based subtype-oriented classification.
venue: IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics

title: A five-gene risk model based on carnitine-related genes for predicting prognosis in ovarian cancer
abstract: Background: Ovarian cancer (OV) remains a highly lethal gynecological malignancy and is associated with unfavorable long-term outcomes. Carnitine participates in metabolic adaptation of tumor cells by modulating fatty acid oxidation and redox balance. This study sought to identify carnitine-associated prognostic biomarkers in OV and to characterize the molecular features linked to these markers. Methods: Publicly available datasets were used throughout the study.

title: Establishing Oxime as a Bioresponsive Group on Naphthalene Diimide: Visual Bacterial Classification and NIR-II Photothermal Antibacterial
abstract: Bioresponsive groups are fundamental tools in engineering activatable constructs. Herein, we first demonstrated that the oxime group was a bioresponsive group by designing oxime-naphthalene diimide (NONDI). The oxime group could be reduced to an iminyl group by bacteria, and NONDI was completely converted into iminyl-naphthalene diimide (NHNDI). Mechanistically, that reduction triggered homolytic cleavage of the N–O bond in the oxime group and released a hydroxyl radical.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Phenol-Driven Modulation Enables the Crystallization of Titanium Metal–Organic Frameworks
abstract: Titanium-based metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) remain among the most challenging frameworks to synthesize due to the high reactivity of Ti(IV) precursors, particularly when in combination with strongly coordinating phenolate ligands. Phenol is an untapped modulator for MOF synthesis that enabled the formation of a new crystalline Ti-MOF phase, otherwise unattainable through established modulators. We show how transient Ti-phenolate species formed in solution regulate titanium coordination equilibria and demonstrate the broader applicability of phenol modulation for several reported Ti-MOF systems. As a result of phenol modulation, we isolate a previously elusive crystalline titanium ellagate sustainable MOF, TUW-11, composed of monometallic Ti(IV) centers and plant-derived ellagic acid linkers. Three-dimensional electron diffraction, synchrotron X-ray techniques, and scanning transmission electron microscopy reveal a layered microporous framework with 1.1 nm channels. TUW-11 exhibits a narrow band gap, p-type semiconducting behavior, and ligand-centered visible-light photoresponse. These findings demonstrate phenol modulation as a powerful strategy for controlling titanium-phenolate framework formation and expand the synthetic toolbox available for Ti-MOF discovery.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Frontier Orbital Engineering of the Oxide Photocatalyst K2Zn2Nb4O13 by Coupling Crystal Structure, Electronic Structure, and Chemical Bonding
abstract: Rational design of oxide photocatalysts with intrinsically efficient bulk carrier transport remains a major challenge because carrier migration is strongly governed by the complex interplay among crystal structure, electronic structure, and chemical bonding. Here, we propose a Frontier orbital engineering strategy to regulate intrinsic carrier transport by reconstructing the Frontier orbital composition within a structurally robust oxide framework.

title: Artificial intelligence applications in microbiota-gut-brain axis research: Implications for Alzheimer's disease
abstract: Alterations in the gut microbiota (GM) are increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis through the microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA), influencing neuroinflammation, amyloid-β deposition, and tau aggregation. The inherent complexity of microbiota data necessitates artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) to identify novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets. In this narrative review, we examined AI applications in AD-related GM research, including metataxonomic and metagenomic approaches.

title: Constructing the Transfer Ladder between Active Sites and Functional Units within the Cluster-Based Catalyst for Reductive Amination
abstract: The remote communication between active sites and the surrounding environment within a heterogeneous catalyst for the orderly bonding of reactive species is highly desired yet very challenging. Here we find that the phosphotungstate with a mesoporous framework (abbreviated as mPTA) has an extraordinary ability to accommodate ammonia but has no activity for catalytic reductive amination, while the Pd3(S-Adm)3(PPh3)3+ (Pd3 for short; S-Adm = 1-adamantanethiol) cluster enables the above reaction but insufficient ammonia occurring on the cluster leads to low activity and inferior selectivity.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Ammonium thiocyanate enables in-situ structural templating of MAPbI3 via quasi-2D perovskite scaffold
abstract: Ammonium thiocyanate (NH4SCN) has been used extensively to improve the current extraction and device performance of quasi-two-dimensional perovskite solar cells. Whilst this additive has been shown to influence quasi-2D perovskite crystallisation, a detailed understanding of its mechanism has not yet been established. Through spectroscopic and structural studies, we demonstrate that NH4SCN enables quasi-2D perovskite phases to structurally template the dominant 3D phase. Contrary to previous reports, we suggest that the benefit of this additive comes from an improvement to the 3D perovskite structure, not from charges transferring through vertically oriented 2D perovskite layers. We show that this additive provides kinetic control over the quasi-2D phase formation, suppressing the unfavourable n = 1 perovskite phase and promoting the growth of high-n 2D scaffold phases by extending the nucleation window. This promotes the in-situ templated growth of MAPbI3. We provide robust structural analysis demonstrating highly (110)-ordered 3D perovskite, with the mechanism confirmed by close lattice matching between this phase and quasi-2D phases. Furthermore, we show that this structural control is cation dependent, requiring both close lattice matching between quasi-2D and 3D perovskite phases, and successful kinetic control of the relevant quasi-2D phases.

title: Excitons in solid molecular hydrogen from quantum Monte Carlo
abstract: We use quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods to investigate the lowest neutral excitation of solid molecular hydrogen in phase-I under increasing compression, with emphasis on structural and response properties. We employ QMC wave functions for the excited state that feature only a single orbital substitution, or a multideterminant expansion including every single particle-hole transition, and compare the results with the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) and time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT). We examine a number of nuclear configurations representing thermal and quantum fluctuations. The effect of the multideterminant expansion is marginal on the QMC excitation energies but crucial on the exciton localization and related quantities, irrespective of full optimization and imaginary time projection. In the strong insulating regime at low density, multideterminant QMC results match and in some cases surpass the degree of localization afforded by BSE. A similar trend is observed for transition dipole moments and excitation-induced forces, with generally good agreement between QMC and BSE but marked discrepancies for nuclear configurations where localization differs significantly. TDDFT generally gives a more extended exciton with correspondingly weaker transition dipole moments. These differences decrease upon compression, as the system approaches a semiconducting regime where multiple particle-hole transitions are less important.

title: TACFormer: Transformer-Based Generative Model for Target-Conditioned De Novo PROTAC Design
abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) represents a fundamental shift in drug discovery, moving beyond traditional target inhibition toward the event-driven removal of disease-causing proteins. A prominent strategy for TPD is the use of proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), heterobifunctional molecules that selectively route a protein of interest (POI) to the ubiquitin-proteasome system for degradation. While PROTAC design still relies heavily on trial-and-error synthesis and experimental testing, deep generative models offer a promising means to explore PROTAC chemical space in silico and generate novel molecules. However, many existing generative methods formulate PROTAC design primarily as a linker-generation problem, with POI-binding (warhead) and E3-ligase-binding components fixed in advance. This restricts exploration of the full PROTAC chemical space and often leaves the POI implicit through the predefined warhead, rather than using protein-level information as an explicit conditioning signal during generation. To address these limitations, we propose TACFormer: a transformer-based generative model for target-aware de novo PROTAC design. The model conditions a GPT-style molecular decoder on pretrained ESM-2 representations of POI sequences, allowing POI-level information to steer full-molecule generation. Our results show that TACFormer generates highly novel and chemically diverse PROTACs while showing consistent POI-dependent shifts in generated chemical space. In particular, molecules generated under specific target conditions preferentially populate chemical neighborhoods associated with POIs in the held-out dataset, while extrapolating to novel chemotypes. By natively integrating biological context into the generative process, TACFormer moves PROTAC design toward a more biology-informed exploration of degrader chemical space.

title: Epitaxial Magnon Junctions with Y3Fe5O12/Gd3Ga5O12/Pt-nanoparticles/Y3Fe5O12
abstract: The excitation, propagation, manipulation, and detection of magnons lie at the core of magnonics. Among various device architectures, high-quality magnon junctions with a ferromagnetic insulator (FI)/antiferromagnetic insulator (AFI)/ferromagnetic insulator (FI) configuration are predicted to exhibit a near-100% magnon junction ratio (MJR), making them promising candidates for high-performance non-volatile memory applications. Yttrium iron garnet (Y3Fe5O12, YIG) is widely employed as the FI material in such structures for its exceptionally low magnetic damping. However, in previously reported magnon junctions, the epitaxial relationship between the two YIG layers is often disrupted by lattice-mismatched AFI spacers. Although this leads to distinct coercivities, it simultaneously degrades the crystalline quality of the top YIG layer, thereby limiting the magnontransmission efficiency. Here, an epitaxial magnon junction is demonstrated incorporating a hybrid Gd3Ga5O12 (GGG)/Pt-nanoparticles spacer that maintains coherent epitaxy while enabling an antiparallel magnetic configuration. Compared with nickel oxide-based magnon junctions, the coercivity-tuned top YIG layer in our structure exhibits superior crystalline quality and much lower magnetic damping. A clear magnon junction effect is observed with a 43% MJR achieved. The interlayer coupling between the two ferrimagnetic insulators is found to enhance the MJR. These results offer valuable insights for the development of advanced magnon-based spintronic devices.

title: Steering interfacial molecular structures by substrate-molecule charge transfer
abstract: Intermixed self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) provide a powerful approach for tuning inorganic-organic interfaces, but their local structure and energetics often remain elusive. Here, an intermixed stripe phase of fullerene $C_{60}$ and Zn(II)-5,10,15,20-tetrakis(4-aminophenyl)porphyrin (Zn-TAPP) on a Ag(111) surface is identified, establishing a direct link between molecular assembly and charge transfer. Scanning tunnelling spectroscopy (STS) and Kelvin probe force spectroscopy (KPFS) have been used to map electronic states and local contact potential differences (LCPD). Compared to close-packed $C_{60}$ islands, the stripe phase exhibits a larger interfacial dipole and increased occupation of previously unoccupied $C_{60}$ states, consistent with enhanced charge transfer from Ag(111) to $C_{60}$. Analysis indicates that larger $C_{60}$ spacing in the stripe geometry reduces Coulomb repulsion, stabilizing the intermixed phase and enhancing charge transfer with respect to close-packed domains. These results provide direct evidence of charged $C_{60}$ molecules in stripe structures and guidelines for engineering intermixed SAMs with tailored interfacial electronic properties.

title: Interpreting Graph Neural Networks for Antibacterial Drug Repurposing against Acinetobacter baumannii
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in Acinetobacter baumannii, whose carbapenem-resistant strains are classified by the World Health Organization as a critical priority, has motivated machine-learning screens for new antibacterials, but translating predictions into chemical hypotheses requires evaluating the molecular features on which a model relies. A graph neural network ensemble achieves competitive predictive performance against a descriptor-augmented reference model on the same antibacterial screen while using only atom features and connectivity, allowing interpretation to focus on the molecular…

title: Strategies and tools for enhancing early detection of pancreatic cancer
abstract: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAC) remains the most lethal malignancies, with a 5-year survival rate of only around 12%. The dismal prognosis is largely attributable to late diagnosis, as early PAC is frequently asymptomatic and radiologically inconspicuous. Contemporary international guidelines recommend surveillance for well-defined high-risk groups, particularly carriers of pathogenic germline mutations such as BRCA2, STK11, and CDKN2A, as well as familial pancreatic cancer kindreds.
venue: Journal of the Formosan Medical Association = Taiwan yi zhi

title: Webserver Integrated Machine Learning Platform for Predicting Polymer Imprinting Factors in Cancer Therapeutics
abstract: Molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) is a class of synthetic receptors capable of specifically recognizing and binding target molecules by forming a molecularly defined binding site. These polymers have been known for its application in drug delivery, clinical diagnosis and biosensing. However, the design and optimization of MIP systems often require extensive experimental trial and error. In this work, we attempted to develop a webserver for the computational design, optimization, visualization of anticancer drug-based MIP systems.

title: Chemical recycling turns silicone waste into reusable building blocks with up to 99% yield
abstract: Silicones are widely used in industry, medicine and everyday products due to their exceptional thermal and chemical stability. However, it is precisely these properties that have made recycling silicones extremely problematic in the past. Researchers at the Institute of Chemistry at TU Berlin have now succeeded in breaking down the polymer chains of silicone molecules into their basic building blocks. The resulting molecule dimethyldichlorosilane can then be reused as a starting material for the production of new silicone compounds.

title: Multiscale Spatial Characterization of Glioma MRI with MUSE and Radiomics
abstract: Purpose: Characterizing glioma heterogeneity requires measurements that retain the physical scale and orientation of intratumoral intensity dependence. We evaluate the original 3D variographic field produced by the MUSE tool (Modeling Uncertainty as a Support for the Environment) alongside directional radiomics and independent image-based molecular classification. Methods. We analyzed postcontrast T1-weighted magnetic resonance images and enhancing-tumor segmentations from the public UCSF-PDGM collection.

title: Electrochemical functionalization of graphene rationalized by Hammett and Swain-Lupton parameters
abstract: Graphene's sp^{2}-bonded carbon lattice makes it exceptionally resistant to covalent functionalization, with existing approaches relying on chemically specific and often harsh methods, fragmenting our understanding of its reactivity. Here we show that electric fields of approximately 1 V nm^{-1} in non-aqueous electrolytes enable the electrochemical functionalization of monolayer graphene with a broad range of substituents, leading to two-order-of-magnitude conductance modulation stable over 5,000 cycles and semi-reversible electronic conductor-insulator transitions. Analysis of the oxidation potentials across substituents reveals trends governed by classical descriptors. Species forming localised σ bonds display increasing oxidation potentials with the meta-Hammett constant (σ_m), whereas substituents interacting via delocalised π orbitals follow an inverse dependence on the modified Swain-Lupton resonance parameter (R). These relationships indicate that graphene's oxidation potential increases with the electron-withdrawing strength of the substituent. Our results provide new insights into the electrochemical activity of inert materials under strong electric fields.

title: Unraveling the Ultrafast Photodynamics of Molecular Photoswitches in β-Adrenergic Receptors by First-Principles Nonadiabatic Dynamics Simulations
abstract: Understanding how protein environments regulate the photodynamics of chromophores is a central task in quantum biology and remains a major challenge. This challenge is particularly significant for G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), which are natively nonphotochromic but can be optically controlled via synthetic photoswitchable ligands. Such artificial photoreceptors are new and important because they not only enable the photocontrol of signaling processes beyond those regulated by rhodopsins but also deepen our fundamental understanding of quantum effects in light-protein interactions. However, the ultrafast nonadiabatic dynamics of these ligands in GPCRs remain difficult to resolve experimentally, while traditional computational approaches fail to describe these processes accurately and efficiently. Here, we employed a multiscale framework to comprehensively characterize how receptor binding, mutations, receptor subtype, chemical substitution, and binding pocket electrostatics regulate the photodynamics of photoswitchable antagonists (OPs) of β-adrenergic receptors (β-ARs). This framework integrates extensive first-principles ground-state conformational sampling, absorption-spectra calculations, and nonadiabatic dynamics simulations. Chemical substitutions influence how excitation energy, excited-state lifetimes, and quantum yields (QY) respond to receptor binding, subtype changes, and binding-pocket mutations. The F289A and Y199A mutants generally accelerate excited-state dynamics by reducing local contacts, whereas the D113E mutation slows the dynamics of OP2 in β2-ΑR by reducing the excited-state driving force. Neutralizing the charge of the counterion D113 residue via protonation increases the QY of OP2 in β2-ΑR by altering the local electrostatic and hydrogen-bonding environment. The ultrafast photoisomerization of the ligands does not require large binding-pocket expansion. Overall, this work provides new insights into how binding-pocket environments regulate the photochemical properties of photoswitchable ligands targeting GPCRs.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Measuring multiple reactions on a single electrode with extraordinary sensitivity
abstract: A reaction on a single electrode can tell scientists a remarkable amount about the chemical nature and number of analytes involved. The challenge comes when they want to distinguish many reactions on the same electrode. After more than a decade of trying to overcome that limitation, Ravi Saraf and his Nebraska Engineering graduate students have demonstrated a way to quantify many reactions on the same electrode without sacrificing extraordinary sensitivity.

title: CASCADE: continuous wavelet transform-Adam spectral curve-fitting and decomposition engine for bio-Raman peak fitting
abstract: Omics technologies have transformed biology but remain destructive, static, and incompatible with longitudinal measurements in living systems. Raman fingerprint spectroscopy offers a compelling noninvasive omics surrogate. Broadband coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (BCARS) reveals coordinated biochemical changes in proteins, lipids, and metabolites at information densities comparable to transcriptomics, with subcellular spatial resolution and millisecond acquisition times.

title: Pre-Refinement Prediction of Dopant Site Occupancy in M-Type Hexaferrites via Hierarchical and Uncertainty-Aware Machine-Learning
abstract: Dopant site occupancy bridges chemical composition, local crystal structure, and macroscopic functional responses in M-type hexaferrites. However, reliable occupancy hypotheses are difficult to establish before structural refinement. Here, we develop a pre-refinement machine-learning framework using 494 dopant-level records extracted from refined structures. This workflow combines Ba/Sr-vs.-Fe sublattice classification, fractional occupancy prediction over five inequivalent Fe sites, and reliability-aware assessment.

title: Machine learning-assisted serum Raman spectroscopy for risk stratification in men with suspected prostate cancer: a retrospective proof-of-concept study
abstract: Background: Serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) remains the principal laboratory investigation for men with suspected prostate cancer but has limited specificity, particularly in patients with PSA concentrations between 4 and 10 ng/mL. Additional blood-based tests capable of improving risk stratification before imaging or biopsy could reduce unnecessary investigations while maintaining diagnostic sensitivity.

title: Serum Raman spectroscopy as a blood-based triage test for bladder cancer: a retrospective proof-of-concept study
abstract: Background: Bladder cancer remains one of the most common urological malignancies. Current diagnostic pathways rely heavily on cystoscopy, an invasive investigation with significant cost and resource implications. A rapid blood-based assay capable of improving patient stratification before cystoscopy could reduce unnecessary invasive investigations while maintaining diagnostic sensitivity. Methods Archived serum samples from patients with histologically confirmed bladder cancer and symptomatic control subjects were analysed using dried-serum Raman spectroscopy.

title: Giant Magneto-Photoresponse in 2D Room-Temperature Magnetic Semiconductor Heterostructures
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) magnetic semiconductor heterostructures serve as an ideal material platform for the exploration of emergent physical phenomena and high-density integrated electronics, owing to the strong magneto-electric-optical coupling at their interfaces. Remarkably, the interfacial engineering also endows the heterosystem with pronounced multifield tunability, facilitating the development of next-generation low-power multifunctional devices. Nevertheless, their practical development remains hindered by low magnetic ordering temperatures and the lack of scalable synthetic methods.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Phase Separation of Intracellular Proteins Influences Synaptic Bistability
abstract: Synaptic bistability at the post synaptic density has been proposed to be the result of the nucleation and evaporation of receptor clusters. The exact biophysical mechanism underlying these inter-receptor attractions that can trigger nucleation remains to be elucidated. Emerging evidence demonstrates that numerous postsynaptic density submembrane proteins, that interact with various membrane receptors, can undergo phase separation, necessitating a revised conceptual model. By employing Langevin dynamics simulations of coarse-grained scaffold proteins and interacting membrane receptors, we study how phase transitions of scaffold proteins alter receptor clustering at the membrane. In our model, scaffold macromolecules can undergo phase separation and interact with receptor molecules at the model membranes. We observed that the presence of scaffold polymers across the membrane creates an attractive interaction between otherwise purely repulsive receptors. By systematically varying the number of receptors at the membrane, we dissected the coupling between receptor clustering and the phase behavior of scaffold macromolecules. We show that the propensity for receptor clustering is enhanced by the condensation of scaffold proteins. We then used two different scaffolds and systematically varied the interaction between them, to change the spatial organization of two condensed phases w.r.t. one another. Interestingly, we observed that receptor clustering can be reduced by co-phase separation of scaffold macromolecules, indicating the role of competing interactions in receptor clustering. Our work advances understanding of receptor-mediated signaling and phase separation, providing insights into cellular compartmentalization and biochemical regulation at the synapse.

title: Rugnux: from diffraction images to structure at synchrotrons and XFELs in one program
abstract: Rising data rates in macromolecular crystallography outpace multi-program pipelines on computing clusters. Rugnux, a single GPU-accelerated program, turns rotation or serial still diffraction images into merged data and an initial structure. At synchrotrons, results arrive seconds after the last image; on one workstation, 207 public datasets from 36 sources took a median of 15 s each, with deposition-quality. Serial XFEL data were processed faster than the collection rate, enabling real-time structure determination.

title: A mechanistic classification of GNAO1 mutations links Gβ γ sequestration to hyperkinetic disease and treatment response
abstract: Go is the most prevalent G protein subunit in the brain and is critical for signal transduction through G protein-coupled receptors. Mutations in the gene encoding Go (GNAO1) cause a rare neurodevelopmental disorder with involuntary movements (NEDIM) and, in some patients, developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). Here, we integrate human genetic analysis with cellular assays to define mechanistic classes of GNAO1 mutations and in vivo approaches to evaluate therapeutic strategies.

title: A Synthetic Virology Platform for Rapid Prototyping of Influenza A Virus mutants
abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) remains a significant public health threat, with the need for effective vaccines and antiviral therapies remaining a high priority. In vitro testing is paramount in studying novel IAV viruses and their immunogenicity. To address this need, we developed a synthetic virology approach to rapidly prototype and test IAV mutants with altered antigenic sites. By strategically inserting restriction sites within an ambisense plasmid, we generated a tool where we can seamlessly replace either 1) the full hemagglutinin (HA), 2) the HA globular head domain to generate head/stalk chimeras or 3) the five canonical antigenic sites. The cloning inserts can be computationally designed and artificially synthesized, enabling rescue of synthetic Influenza A viruses. Using this platform we rescued IAV H1N1, H3N2 & H5N1, and went on to prototype their respective antigenic site mutants & chimeric IAVs using viral genome sequence alone. This platform could be useful for generating vaccine seed strains or to study anti-viral immunity.
